# Calling Parent Methods in Overridden Functions

When you override a method in a child class like `User`, the default behavior is to execute your new implementation completely, ignoring what lies beneath it in the parent class `BaseUser`. This is how inheritance and polymorphism are meant to work. However, there are specific scenarios where you need to retain the original logic of the parent while adding your own custom behavior before or after it runs.

In your case, you have defined a `delete` method in the `User` class that currently does nothing. If you simply want to execute the parent's delete functionality but also perform some cleanup tasks specific to your `User` model, you must explicitly invoke the parent's method.

## The Syntax for Invoking Parent Methods

To call the `delete` function from the `BaseUser` class within the `User` class, you use the `parent::` prefix followed by the method name. This is a standard mechanism in object-oriented programming languages like PHP, allowing you to access inherited members that might otherwise be shadowed.

Here is how your code should look:

```php
class User extends BaseUser {
    public function delete() {
        // Perform custom logic before deletion
        $this->logDeletionRequest();
        
        // Call the parent's delete implementation
        return parent::delete(); 
    }
}
```

In this example, when you execute `$user->delete()`, PHP executes your code inside the `User` class first. It logs the request (whatever that entails in your application), and then it calls `parent::delete()`. This ensures that the core deletion logic defined in `BaseUser` is not bypassed.

## Returning Values and Side Effects

It is crucial to consider what your overridden method returns. In Laravel, the `Model` trait provides a default implementation for `delete` that returns `true` on success or `false` on failure. If you override this method without calling the parent, you break the contract expected by other parts of your application.

If your custom logic in `User::delete()` throws an exception or returns a specific status code before calling the parent, ensure that the return value of `parent::delete()` is propagated correctly. Failing to pass the result back can lead to silent failures where the database record remains untouched even though your code thinks it was deleted.

## Common Pitfalls in Inheritance Chains

Your project structure mentions a separate `UserTable` class. It is important to clarify how this fits into the inheritance hierarchy. If `UserTable` is intended to be an Eloquent model (or a custom implementation of one), it should extend `BaseUser`, not exist alongside it as a separate table definition object.

If you are using the Laravel framework, the standard practice is to define your models in files like `App\Models\User.php`. The class name usually matches the database table name (excluding the prefix). Ensure that `BaseUser` contains the actual logic for deletion and that `User` extends it correctly.

Attempting to call the parent method without the `parent::` keyword will result in a fatal error because PHP cannot find a method named `delete` within the current class scope if only your version exists there. Always verify that the parent class actually defines the method you intend to override; otherwise, the inheritance chain is incomplete.

## When Not to Override

Before deciding to override `delete`, ask yourself if you truly need to intercept the process. Sometimes it is cleaner to use event listeners or hooks provided by the framework (like Laravel's `deleted` event) to handle custom logic after the record is removed. Overriding core methods like `delete` can make debugging difficult and may cause issues if you upgrade your base library or framework version, as internal implementations might change.

If you find yourself frequently needing to customize delete behavior, consider whether a trait or an interface would provide a more maintainable solution than direct method overriding in every child class.
